reader_situation: A reader is standing in the cleaning aisle, or looking at a crowded cabinet, and wants to know which surface-specific bottles actually prevent damage and which are the same job under a different label. Many also wonder whether one disinfecting spray can do everything.
direct_answer: Usually not. A mild detergent or all-purpose cleaner, a glass cleaner, and an EPA-registered disinfectant used only where it's needed cover most of a home. A dedicated product earns a spot only where the everyday products cause damage. The sources here point to four such places: marble and other calcium-based stone, finished wood floors, glass-ceramic cooktops, and leather. For leather, the main need is keeping the wrong products off it. Granite and stainless steel don't need their own bottle, but they each have products to keep away.
consensus: Most surfaces can be cleaned with an all-purpose cleaner or dish soap and water.
Natural stone needs a pH-neutral cleaner because acids such as vinegar and lemon can damage it.
Hardwood floors need a wood floor cleaner, not a wet mop.
Never mix bleach with ammonia or acids.
gaps: Not all 'natural stone' reacts to acid the same way. The Natural Stone Institute says calcareous stones (marble, limestone, travertine) are sensitive to acids, while siliceous stones like granite are 'generally resistant to most acids found in kitchen settings.' Acidic cleaners are still not recommended on either.

Sealing does not protect marble from acid. The Natural Stone Institute says a sealer 'does nothing to protect etching, no matter how much sealer you use'; it only slows staining. Etching shows more on polished than on honed marble.

The stone hazard most people miss is in the bathroom aisle. The Natural Stone Institute says some rust removers and toilet bowl cleaners contain hydrofluoric acid, and all stones, including granite and quartzite, are attacked by it.

Granite doesn't strictly need a branded stone cleaner. The Natural Stone Institute lists a neutral cleaner, stone soap, or mild dishwashing detergent and warm water, but warns that too much soap leaves a film and streaks. Its granite article quotes a stone expert who prefers a stone cleaner because soap can leave a dulling film.

The 'disinfect everything' habit is a stainless steel risk. Consumer Reports advises against disinfectants, abrasives, and cleaners containing bleach, alcohol, ammonia, or chlorides on stainless appliances. GE says not to use bleach or other chlorine products, appliance wax, or polish on stainless.

Disinfecting is a situational step, not a daily one. CDC says cleaning regularly is enough in most situations and disinfecting is likely not needed unless someone at home is sick or has a weakened immune system.

A glass cleaner can't double as a cooktop cleaner if it contains ammonia. Whirlpool says not to use steel wool, abrasive powder cleansers, chlorine bleach, rust remover, or ammonia on ceramic glass cooktops, and to use a cooktop scraper and ceramic cooktop cleaner.

Saddle soap, sold as a leather product, is on a leather furniture maker's do-not-use list. American Leather says routine care is dry dusting and vacuuming, and lists saddle soap, solvents, furniture polish, oils, detergent soaps, and ammonia water as products not to use.
The old article's cost figures ($3-5 vs $6-9 per bottle, $50-100 a year, a $10 stone cleaner) and the '90% of the job' line have no source and were removed.

evidence.detail: Products containing lemon, vinegar or other acids may dull or etch calcareous stones. Calcium carbonate is sensitive to acidic solutions so mild, non-acidic cleaners are recommended.
evidence.source_title: Natural Stone Institute - Learn About Cleaning Products for Natural Stone

evidence.claim: Granite and other siliceous stones tolerate kitchen acids better
evidence.detail: A siliceous stone is generally resistant to most acids found in kitchen settings; acidic cleaners are still not recommended because siliceous stones may contain acid-sensitive trace minerals.
evidence.source_title: Natural Stone Institute - Learn About Cleaning Products for Natural Stone

evidence.claim: Hydrofluoric acid in some rust removers and toilet bowl cleaners attacks all stone
evidence.detail: Some rust removers and toilet bowl cleaners contain trace hydrofluoric acid; all stones, including granite and quartzite, will be attacked if exposed to HF.
evidence.source_title: Natural Stone Institute - Learn About Cleaning Products for Natural Stone

evidence.detail: Clean stone surfaces with a neutral cleaner, stone soap, or a mild liquid dishwashing detergent and warm water; an excessive concentration of cleaner or soap may leave a film and cause streaks. Scouring powders or creams often contain abrasives that may scratch certain stones.
evidence.source_title: Natural Stone Institute - Learn About Cleaning Products for Natural Stone

evidence.claim: Granite: neutral cleaner, soap film caution, sealer life, water test
evidence.detail: Wipe daily with a neutral cleaner; granite is not sensitive to most common household acids. A stone expert says soap has a fatty acid that leaves a greasy film that can dull or streak. A good sealer can last up to 10 years with the right daily cleaners; improper cleaners can break sealer down. Water test: hot water on an area for 10 to 20 minutes; if the stone darkens it is still absorbing moisture.
evidence.source_title: Caring for Granite Countertops | Natural Stone Institute (usenaturalstone.org)

evidence.claim: Sealing does not stop marble etching
evidence.detail: Etching looks like a dull spot or burn mark from acids such as tomatoes, citrus, juices, alcohol, and vinegar. A sealer does nothing to protect etching, no matter how much sealer you use. Etching shows more on polished marble than honed or textured. Use a mild soap or stone cleaner.
evidence.source_title: How to Care for Your Marble Countertops | Natural Stone Institute (usenaturalstone.org)

evidence.claim: Wood floors need a cleaner made for their finish; no wet or steam mops
evidence.detail: Use a cleaner made specifically for the finish on the floor, which a flooring professional can recommend. Don't use wet mops or steam mops, which will damage the finish and the wood over long periods of time. Clean spills immediately with a dry or slightly damp cloth.
evidence.source_title: Maintenance | National Wood Flooring Association | NWFA

evidence.claim: Ceramic glass cooktops: what to avoid and what to use
evidence.detail: Do not use steel wool, abrasive powder cleansers, chlorine bleach, rust remover, or ammonia. Remove residue with a scraper designed for a ceramic glass cooktop held at about a 45 degree angle, apply a few dime-sized drops of ceramic glass cooktop cleaner, then polish with a clean, dry cloth or paper towel.
evidence.source_title: Cleaning Ceramic Glass Cooktops - Product Help | Whirlpool

evidence.claim: GE: no bleach, chlorine, wax, or polish on stainless
evidence.detail: Do not clean with appliance wax, polish, bleach or other products containing chlorine on stainless steel; GE suggests stainless steel polishing wipes.
evidence.source_title: Missed Spring Cleaning? GE's Appliance Cleaning Tips Help You Get Back on Track in Time for Summer Entertaining

evidence.claim: Stainless appliances can rust; disinfectants and chlorides are on the avoid list
evidence.detail: Avoid disinfectants, abrasives, or cleaners that contain bleach, alcohol, ammonia, or chlorides; bleach-heavy cleaners can cause corrosion in crevices where cleaner is trapped. Avoid steel wool and scrub pads, and don't use a used dishrag. Wash with mild soap and a soft cloth, rinse, and dry; stainless cleaners mostly contain mineral oil that helps protect the steel.
evidence.source_title: Yes, Your Stainless Steel Appliances Can Rust | Consumer Reports

evidence.claim: Cleaning is enough most of the time; disinfect when someone is sick
evidence.detail: In most situations, cleaning regularly is enough to prevent the spread of germs. Disinfecting is likely not needed unless there are sick people in your home, or someone has a weakened immune system. Clean with soap and water first; the surface should stay wet during the entire contact time. Do not mix products or chemicals with each other.
evidence.source_title: When and How to Clean and Disinfect Your Home | CDC

evidence.claim: Leather furniture: dry care, and a do-not-use list that includes saddle soap
evidence.detail: Regular dry-cloth dusting and vacuum cleaning in crevices are all that is necessary. Do not use saddle soap, cleaning solvents, furniture polish, oils, varnish, abrasive cleaners, detergent soaps, or ammonia water. For deeper cleaning, a mild non-detergent soap with lukewarm water after testing a hidden area; for minor spills, a soft cloth lightly moistened with distilled water, then air dry.
evidence.source_title: How to Clean Your Furniture | American Leather

original_asset.spec: Surface-by-surface table: what the source says damages it, what the source says to use, and whether that means a separate bottle. Rows: marble/limestone/travertine, granite/quartzite, finished wood floor, ceramic glass cooktop, stainless appliances, leather furniture, plus a row for disinfectant use. Followed by a 'fussiest surface' shelf check.

cautions: Never mix bleach with ammonia or acids (registry: poison.org).
Disinfectants need an EPA registration number and the full label contact time (registry: EPA).
Some toilet bowl cleaners and rust removers contain hydrofluoric acid: keep them off stone and follow label safety directions.
Check the appliance or floor manufacturer's manual; it overrides general advice and can affect warranties.
